props.title: Dogs
props.initialSlug: When man's best friend turns worst.

sections.content: The vicious canine horror wave of the 1970s peaked with **Dogs (1976)** (1976), riding the wake of **Jaws** (1975) success. Director Burt Brinckerhoff tapped into post-Vietnam paranoia by turning man's best friend into a savage killing machine. The film follows a college professor investigating why local dogs suddenly turn murderous. While lacking the polish of later killer dog films like Cujo (1983), Dogs captures raw 70s exploitation energy with its pack attacks and environmental horror undertones.

sections.content: The killer dog subgenre evolved significantly through the 1980s and 90s. **Man's Best Friend** (1993) added genetic engineering to the mix with its escaped lab experiment premise. **The Breed** (2006) modernized pack dynamics by focusing on trained attack dogs. But the thoughtful exploration of human-canine relationships in White Dog (1982) stands apart, using the killer dog premise to confront racism and conditioning. SUBHEAD: Beyond Simple Horror

Recent films have moved past pure horror to examine deeper bonds between humans and dogs, even in dark scenarios. **The Thing** (1982) uses dogs as both victims and vectors of alien infection, playing on our trust of pets. **Eight Below** (2006) flips the script entirely - instead of dogs as threats, they become heroes fighting brutal conditions. This evolution shows how the killer dog concept has expanded into more nuanced territory.
